prompt: What decides which shard of a stream a record is written to?
hint: The producer supplies one string with every record.

choices.text: The MD5 of its partition key
choices.why: Right. The digest is read as a 128-bit number, and each shard owns a contiguous range of them.

choices.text: Kinesis sends each record to the shard with the least data in it
choices.why: Kinesis does no balancing of its own; the key alone decides, which is how a hot shard happens.

choices.text: The shards take records in turn
choices.why: A rotation would scatter one customer's events over every shard and lose their order.

choices.text: A hash of the record's data
choices.why: Kinesis never looks inside the data; two different events of one customer go to the same shard.

prompt: A stream created with two shards. The MD5 of a key, read as a number, is 254303140926280561521588452831818067638, which is above 2^127. Where does the record go?
hint: A new stream splits the space in half.

choices.text: To shard 0, because shard 0 is filled first
choices.why: Shards are not filled in order; each owns a range of the hash space.

choices.text: To shard 1
choices.why: Right. Shard 1 owns 2^127 and everything above it. That number is the MD5 of `c-02`, which the lesson put on shard 1.

choices.text: It is refused, because the number is larger than a 64-bit integer
choices.why: The hash key space is 128 bits wide; every MD5 fits in it.

choices.text: To either shard, chosen when the record arrives
choices.why: The same key always lands on the same shard; that is what keeps a key in order.

prompt: Quitanda keys its order stream by store. It has three stores, and the stream has eight shards. What happens?
hint: Count the distinct hash values.

choices.text: Eight shards share the load evenly, one store per shard and the rest idle in reserve
choices.why: Shards in reserve do not take over anything; idle is all they are.

choices.text: Kinesis notices the skew and spreads the three keys over all eight shards
choices.why: Nothing rebalances keys; the hash decides, and three keys give three hashes.

choices.text: At most three shards receive records, and the other five are paid for and idle
choices.why: Right. Three keys hash to three points; a key with more values, such as the customer, would spread.

choices.text: The stream refuses keys with fewer values than shards
choices.why: Kinesis accepts any key; it never knows how many distinct values you will send.

prompt: A producer that wants to name a point on the hash line itself, instead of letting Kinesis hash the key, passes ___ in `PutRecord`.
hint: Its name says the hash key is given rather than computed.

prompt: The producer wrote `o-101 placed` and then `o-102 placed`, for customers on different shards. What does Kinesis promise about the order a consumer reads them in?
hint: Order is a property of something smaller than the stream.

choices.text: That `o-101 placed` is read first, since it was written first
choices.why: That holds within one shard; these two are on different shards.

choices.text: Nothing: order holds within a shard and not across shards
choices.why: Right. In the lesson the consumer printed `o-102 placed` sixth, after all of shard 0.

choices.text: That they are read in order of `ApproximateArrivalTimestamp`
choices.why: The timestamp is approximate, and no read sorts by it; a reader that wants it has to sort.

choices.text: That they come back in the order of their sequence numbers
choices.why: Sequence numbers are positions in one shard; both of these were number 1 in their own shard.

prompt: Code that tested against moto stores sequence numbers as integers and compares them with `<`. Why will it break on AWS?
hint: What does an AWS sequence number look like?

choices.text: AWS sequence numbers are random, so comparing two with `<` means nothing
choices.why: They increase over time within a shard; comparing them is meaningful.

choices.text: AWS numbers sequence records across the whole stream, not per shard
choices.why: A sequence number is a position in one shard on AWS as in moto.

choices.text: On AWS they are long decimal strings, too large for a 64-bit integer
choices.why: Right. Keep them as strings, and compare them as numbers of arbitrary size.

choices.text: Sequence numbers on AWS start at zero
choices.why: Where they start is not the problem; their size is.

prompt: A producer's `PutRecord` for `o-101 packed` times out, the producer sends it again, and meanwhile it has written `o-101 delivered`. What can the shard now hold?
hint: The producer cannot tell whether the first attempt was written.

choices.text: `packed`, `delivered` and `packed` again: a duplicate, and an event after a later one
choices.why: Right. The first attempt may have been written; the retry adds it again after `delivered`. Lesson 23 deals with it.

choices.text: Only `packed` and `delivered`, in that order, because Kinesis drops repeated records
choices.why: Kinesis does not deduplicate; a retried record gets a new sequence number.

choices.text: Only `delivered`, because the timed-out request is cancelled
choices.why: A timeout on the producer's side cancels nothing on the server.

choices.text: `packed` and `delivered`, sorted by Kinesis by the time they were sent
choices.why: Kinesis keeps the order of arrival in the shard and knows nothing of when a producer sent.

prompt: What does `PutRecords`, which writes up to 500 records in one call, promise about their order?
hint: It is not `PutRecord` with a list.

choices.text: That they are written in the order of the list
choices.why: That is the belief to drop; it makes no such promise.

choices.text: Order within each partition key, but not across keys
choices.why: Even records of one key in one batch may be written out of the list's order.

choices.text: Nothing, not even within its own batch
choices.why: Right. `PutRecord` with `SequenceNumberForOrdering` is the strict form.

prompt: A consumer restarts after an hour down and asks for a `LATEST` iterator. What happens to the records written during that hour?
hint: Where does `LATEST` point?

choices.text: They are delivered first, oldest to newest, and then the new ones follow
choices.why: That would be `AFTER_SEQUENCE_NUMBER` from a checkpoint.

choices.text: They are deleted from the shard
choices.why: Reading or not reading never deletes; only the retention period does.

choices.text: This consumer never sees them; they stay in the shard for other readers
choices.why: Right. `LATEST` points after the newest record, so it sees only what is written once it exists.

choices.text: Kinesis refuses a `LATEST` iterator while unread records remain in the shard
choices.why: Kinesis has no notion of a record being unread; each reader keeps its own position.

prompt: Match each need to the iterator type that serves it.
hint: One of them starts at a time rather than at a record.

pairs.left: Reprocess everything the shard still keeps
Resume after the last record you finished
Only what is written from now on

prompt: A consumer on a stream with the default retention is broken from Friday evening to Monday morning. It is fixed and restarted with `TRIM_HORIZON`. What does it read?
hint: The default retention is a day.

choices.text: Everything since Friday evening, because unread records are kept until somebody reads them
choices.why: A shard keeps records for the retention period, read or not, and then deletes them.

choices.text: Only the last 24 hours; the weekend before that is gone, with no error
choices.why: Right. `TRIM_HORIZON` silently means a later point. Seven days of retention would have saved the weekend.

choices.text: Nothing, because the iterator from Friday has expired
choices.why: A new iterator is taken at restart; expiry only means the old one cannot be reused.

choices.text: An error saying records were lost
choices.why: There is no such error; that silence is the danger.

prompt: What is the largest retention period a Kinesis stream accepts, in hours? moto refused 9,000 with the limit in its message.
hint: 365 days.

prompt: A stream of ten shards is throttled on one shard while the other nine are nearly idle. What helps?
hint: The limit is per shard, and the key decides the shard.

choices.text: A partition key with more values, so the busy key's records spread
choices.why: Right. A hot shard comes from a hot key; adding shards leaves that key where it is.

choices.text: Doubling the shards with `update-shard-count`
choices.why: The busy key still hashes to one point, now in a child shard of half the range.

choices.text: Enhanced fan-out on the consumers
choices.why: That raises reading capacity; the throttle here is on writing.

choices.text: Longer retention
choices.why: Retention decides how long records stay, not how fast they can arrive.

prompt: In the lab, 2,000 records went into a one-shard stream in well under a second with none failing. What does that show?
hint: What does moto keep a clock for?

choices.text: That a shard takes more than 1,000 records a second when they are small
choices.why: The limit is 1 MB or 1,000 records a second, whichever comes first; small records hit the count.

choices.text: That moto applies no capacity limit, so throttling was never tested
choices.why: Right. On AWS part of that would have been refused with `ProvisionedThroughputExceededException`.

choices.text: That `PutRecords` is exempt from the per-shard limit
choices.why: Each record in a batch counts against its shard as a single one would.

prompt: After `update-shard-count` from 2 to 4, a consumer reads shard 3 before shard 0. What goes wrong for the key `c-17`?
hint: Where are c-17's events from before the reshard?

choices.text: Nothing, because shard 3 holds a copy of shard 0's records
choices.why: Children start empty; the parent keeps its records until the retention period removes them.

choices.text: Its events from after the reshard are read before its events from before it
choices.why: Right. A parent must be read to its end before its children, which the Kinesis Client Library does by following `ParentShardId`.

choices.text: Shard 0 refuses reads once it is closed
choices.why: A closed shard refuses writes; it can be read until its records expire.

choices.text: `c-17` moves to shard 1, so its events are split three ways
choices.why: Shard 1 is closed too; `shard_of.py` found `c-17` in shard 3.

prompt: For a steady, known load, the lesson's provisioned stream cost 82.50 a month and the on-demand one 250.40. What does on demand buy for the difference?
hint: What did the promotion month show?

choices.text: Records kept for longer
choices.why: Both start at 24 hours; longer retention is priced separately in each mode.

choices.text: Not having to size and reshard for a peak nobody knows yet
choices.why: Right. Sized for a 30 MB/s peak, the provisioned stream would have cost 657.00 in shard-hours alone.

choices.text: Order across shards
choices.why: An on-demand stream is shards too, and orders records the same way.

choices.text: Reads that cost nothing however many consumers there are
choices.why: The reverse: on demand, every consumer pays the read line again.

prompt: A provisioned stream receives 10 million records a day of 30 KB each, for 30 days. At 0.02800 USD per million PUT payload units of 25 KB, what do the payload units cost in the month, in USD?
hint: A record of 30 KB is two units.

prompt: Quitanda adds a third consumer to the steady stream of the lesson. How does each bill change?
hint: Which mode charges per gigabyte read?

choices.text: Both rise by a third
choices.why: A provisioned stream bills shards, not reads.

choices.text: On demand rises by 48.00; provisioned does not move
choices.why: Right: 600 GB × 0.08000 on demand. Three consumers share 2 MB a second per shard on a provisioned stream, and that is plenty at this load.

choices.text: Provisioned needs a shard per consumer, so it rises by a third; on demand does not move
choices.why: Consumers do not take shards of their own; they share each shard's reading capacity.

choices.text: Neither changes
choices.why: The on-demand bill has a read line per consumer.

prompt: Put in order what happens to `c-17`'s records when the stream of the lesson goes from two shards to four.
hint: The parent is closed before any record lands in a child.
items: Its records are written to shard 0, the shard its MD5 falls in
`update-shard-count` closes shard 0 and opens shards 2 and 3 over its range
New records with the key land in shard 3
A consumer reads shard 0 to its end
The same consumer moves on to shard 3

prompt: A fraud check needs every event of one order in order, and nothing across orders. Customers place many orders a day. Which partition key fits best?
hint: The smallest thing whose events must stay in order.

choices.text: The store, so each store's fraud is checked on one shard
choices.why: Three values put the stream on three shards at most, and nothing asked for store order.

choices.text: The customer
choices.why: It works, but it ties all of a heavy customer's orders to one shard when only each order needs order.

choices.text: A random value per record, to spread the load
choices.why: It spreads perfectly and scatters one order's events over every shard, losing the order needed.

choices.text: The order id
choices.why: Right. It keeps each order in order and spreads better than the customer.

prompt: Which of these did this lesson see moto do as AWS would? Choose all that apply.
hint: Separate what was run from what was only documented.

choices.text: Put a key on the shard its MD5 falls in
choices.why: Right; `shard_of.py` predicted every record.

choices.text: Refuse a retention of 9,000 hours
choices.why: Right, with AWS's own limit in the message.

choices.text: Throttle writes beyond 1,000 records a second on a shard
choices.why: moto accepted 2,000 in well under a second.

choices.text: Delete records older than the retention period
choices.why: moto keeps every record until it stops; the deletion was not run.

choices.text: Close the parent shards when resharding
choices.why: Right; they got an `EndingSequenceNumber`.
